Keep parts availability in mind. Extreme example: my truck is 30 and getting parts can be a nightmare. I couldn't get u-joint yoke stock, I had to have it custom milled out of state. But older vehicles have hidden problems mostly sussed out and public, unlike newer vehicles.

If vehicle has been discontinued, check to see if it used chassis, engine, etc, shared by continued or other plentiful models. The obozo cash for clunkers drove up used car/parts costs bc they destroyed so many older, perfectly good, vehicles.

Try and buy from an individual or a dealer trade in. Avoid used car lots, they buy from auction and often the card have unreported history. We bought truck once for a company I worked for and it had s clean accident record but it wasn’t reported that it was flooded during hurricane Katrina

You would be surprised how many used cars I have looked at that were not full of oil. Check fluid and look at the filters. Fluid should be topped off and filters should look relatively new. Basic maintenance is what keeps a vehicle on the road. If there are service records, even better.

If you live in a climate where there is snow, have a look underneath the vehicle for rust. Inspect the vehicle for things that are obviously dented/damaged or have been replaced (body panels of a different color, for example), which may indicate it has been in an accident. Whenever possible, check the CARFAX report because it goes by the VIN on the vehicle and won't leave out any accidents or problems that are tied to the VIN. Oh, and if they won't let you test drive it and take it to a mechanic to have it inspected prior to purchase, walk away.

Make sure it can pass a state inspection. It's a catch-all check that helps you to identify annoyances. Check ALL lights, turn signals. Check that the windshield doesn't have a crack that will fetch you a ticket. Make sure the tires are not worn beyond the legal limit. Check windshield wiper operation. Etc. Most of those things are minor, but necessary to have in good working order to be legal.

If you can, bring a friend who is familiar with mechanics to check it out with you.

Another good thing to do if you find a car that you are ready to put money on: Ask the owner if you can bring the car to an auto shop for a quick oil change, or tune-up/inspection, that you will pay for. Preferably to a mechanic you know, and trust. Explain to the mechanic that you are looking to buy the car, and ask for his professional opinion on what you are buying, and if there are any issues that he can spot. Most shops will gladly offer this advise as a little extra service, on top of a basic oil change, for little to no extra charge.
